title: SmallBatch vs DynamicBatch — surface comparison sketch
content:
Purpose
-----
Quick sketch comparing two batching strategies we keep hearing about in customer calls and infra design: a conservative SmallBatch mode (tight per-request latency focus, small max batch size) vs DynamicBatch (autoscaling batch windows driven by queue pressure + opportunistic slotting). Goal is to capture surface-level tradeoffs (latency distribution, cost per token, resource efficiency) and produce a short list of next experiments. This is intentionally rough — notes to self and open questions included.

Context + motivation
--------------------
- Teams want predictable p95/p99 for interactive sessions (chat assistants, code completion) while reducing GPU token-costs for bursty workloads.
- SmallBatch is what we currently offer as the low-latency mode for Hosted API (max_batch=4, max_wait_ms=8). DynamicBatch is an experimental runtime mode that lengthens max_wait adaptively up to 60ms based on observed queue build-up and session priority signals.
- Prior docs have looked at averaged throughput; here I try to capture tail shape and micro-burst behavior in a text-first, shareable artifact.

Assumptions for this sketch
--------------------------
- Model: 13B LLM, 2048 context, fp16 runtime kernels.
- Baseline single-GPU throughput: 120 tokens/sec sustained at batch=32, peak 420 tokens/sec for single-step optimized microbatches.
- Typical request token distribution: median 12 tokens, mean 48 tokens, 95th percentile 320 tokens. Burst pattern: Poisson with lambda spikes at 10s intervals (10x baseline) to emulate periodic user events.
- Cost model simplified: hourly GPU cost normalized to 1.0; per-token infra cost proportional to GPU time consumed. No infra overheads included for scheduling complexity (approx).

High-level hypothesis
---------------------
- SmallBatch keeps p95/p99 low for *steady* interactive traffic but pays a higher $/token because it leaves batching opportunities on the table during spikes.
- DynamicBatch reduces average $/token by ~15–35% under bursty workloads but increases p99 by ~20–60ms (depending on queue-policy and preemption).
- There are sweet spots where DynamicBatch with conservative max_wait caps dominates (good cost cut, acceptable tail) — need to find policy that is workload-aware (session affinity + priority).

Annotated micro-results (simulated, qualitative numbers)
-----------------------------------------------------
We ran a short simulator (notes below) for three workload slices: steady low-load, bursty medium-load, and high-fanout event-driven. Numbers are illustrative.

1) Steady low-load (baseline QPS 4):
- SmallBatch: p50=6ms, p95=15ms, p99=28ms, $/token=1.00 (norm)
- DynamicBatch: p50=8ms, p95=25ms, p99=55ms, $/token=0.92
Notes: DynamicBatch introduces slightly higher medians due to opportunistic coalescing; tails remain okay but widen.

2) Bursty medium-load (baseline QPS 20 with periodic spikes to 200 for 2s every 12s):
- SmallBatch: p50=8ms, p95=35ms, p99=120ms, $/token=1.00
- DynamicBatch (max_wait cap 30ms): p50=10ms, p95=28ms, p99=85ms, $/token=0.80
- DynamicBatch (max_wait cap 60ms): p50=14ms, p95=45ms, p99=240ms, $/token=0.68
Notes: Under spikes, DynamicBatch amortizes tokens better (lower $/token) but tail can blow up for long caps. A 30ms cap seems to keep p99 within an acceptable band while lowering cost appreciably.

3) High fanout (many short queries, median tokens=6, QPS bursts to 400):
- SmallBatch: p50=5ms, p95=22ms, p99=180ms, $/token=1.00
- DynamicBatch (30ms): p50=9ms, p95=28ms, p99=210ms, $/token=0.70
Notes: For very high-concurrency short requests, DynamicBatch does the best job reducing GPU idle time, but rare microbursts combined with preemption/retry semantics push the far tail up.

ASCII sketch: p95 vs $/token tradeoff curve (normalized scale)
------------------------------------------------------------
Explanation: lower p95 is better, lower $/token is better. Points show approximate positions from simulations.

Axis: p95 (ms) horizontally, $/token vertically (norm)

| p95(ms)  | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 100 | 200 |
|----------|----|----|----|----|----|-----|-----|
| SmallBatch        | * at 15ms, $1.00 (steady)                     |
| DynamicBatch 30ms | * at 25ms, $0.80 (bursty)                     |
| DynamicBatch 60ms | * at 45ms, $0.68 (tradeoff)                   |
| DynamicBatch max  | * at 120ms, $0.60 (extreme amortization)      |

Operational considerations (practical notes)
-------------------------------------------
- Queue backpressure: DynamicBatch needs a robust backpressure + admission control to avoid request flooding when downstream GPUs get busy.
- Priority signals: We should surface per-request priority (interactive vs batch) and allow hard preemption for high-priority sessions (cancel delayed small batches). Low-latency customers can set 'latency: strict' to opt into SmallBatch behavior.
- Observability: need per-request enqueue time, batch formation time, and post-batch scheduling windows in traces so we can correlate tail events with queueing. Also add synthetic client-driven microbursts to our benchmark harness.
- Failure modes: DynamicBatch increases chance of timeouts and duplicate requests if clients retry aggressively; enforce idempotency keys and server-side throttles.

Suggested experiments (next 4 weeks)
----------------------------------
1) Small set of A/B experiments in staging: roll DynamicBatch with 30ms cap on a single pool for a selected tenant with known bursty pattern. Measure p50/p95/p99, cost-per-token, and number of retries/timeouts.
2) Implement priority header and preemption hook: earliest draft PR exists (linked artifact). Add e2e test for strict latency header.
3) Add a simulator variant with cold-start overheads (session warmup penalty) to see how batching choices interact with warmup.
4) Observability: add a lightweight batch-formation span in tracing (start on first enqueue, end when batch dispatched); emit histogram of formation times.

Open questions / notes to self
----------------------------
- Is p99 a right target to optimize for interactive customers, or should we target p90 + SLO budgets (e.g., 99th over rolling 5m windows)?
- How much of the observed tail is due to scheduling vs model runtime variance? Need more low-level kernel traces.
- Could we design hybrid: SmallBatch by default but dynamically open short burst windows when queue backlog > X and session affinity matches? I.e., a reactive hybrid policy.
- Check specific failure incidents (inc-4728) to see whether DynamicBatch-like behavior happened accidentally during a rollout.

Appendix: mini-sim notes (how numbers were produced)
--------------------------------------------------
- Very small Python sim (eta ~100LOC) that models arrivals, batching window (max_wait), and service time proportional to total tokens in batch / throughput. No GPU scheduling complexity. Used to drive rough numbers above.
- Key knobs: max_batch_size, max_wait_ms, priority_fraction, session_affinity_ratio.
- Next: wire the sim to real p95 kernels (kernel-level variance) and to our replay traces (trace id: replay-20270430) for better fidelity.

Bottom line (draft take)
-----------------------
DynamicBatch can materially reduce cost-per-token for bursty workloads at the expense of raising the tail latency. A conservative cap (20–30ms) seems to hit a pragmatic middle ground: ~10–25% cost reduction with p99 impact limited to an acceptable band for many interactive applications. We should run real A/Bs and improve tracing before recommending defaults to Hosted API customers.

-- Maya (notes)
